title: Plantain Eto
localName: Eto — mashed plantain with palm oil
author: Pamela Owusu
desc: Slightly ripe plantain mashed with red palm oil, ground groundnuts, onion and pepper — the dish given to brides on the morning of a wedding.
longDesc: Eto is mashed starch enriched with palm oil, and it is ceremonial food before it is everyday food. Three slightly ripe plantains and two eggs boil together for half an hour; onions, chillies and roasted groundnuts are ground, with smoked herring and koobi if you have them; sliced onions are heated in palm oil, and the oil goes into the mashed plantain until the whole thing is a deep red-orange. It is served to brides the morning before weddings with eggs, and is described by its author as the local version of a birthday cake.
ingredients: 7 tbsp palm oil — see the note on the quantity
equipment: Earthenware grinding bowl (asanka) and grinder, or a mortar
steps: Boil the plantains and the eggs together with salt for 30 minutes.
Grind the onions, peppers and roasted groundnuts.
Add the smoked herring and koobi, if using, and grind into the mixture in an earthenware bowl.
Mash the plantains separately until smooth.
Heat the sliced onions in 5 to 6 tablespoons of the palm oil.
Mix the palm oil into the mashed plantain.
Combine the mash with the ground mixture.
Garnish with the boiled eggs and sliced avocado, and serve.
chefTips: Slightly ripe, not ripe. Fully ripe plantain goes sweet and sticky and will not take the oil.

The palm oil quantity does not add up as printed — the ingredient list says seven tablespoons, the method uses five to six for the onions and then adds more to the plantain. Treat seven as the total and start with five.
Boil the eggs with the plantains. One pot, and the eggs are part of the dish rather than a garnish.
Grind in an earthenware asanka if you have one. The rough interior does something a blender cannot, and the source specifies it.
Red palm oil, not refined. The colour is the dish — eto without it is just mashed plantain.
The avocado is not optional in practice. Its fat and coolness are what the dish is built against.
Served without salt or pepper when it is being used ceremonially — Osseo-Asare records that the sacred form of the dish is given plain.
commonMistakes: All seven tablespoons of oil into the onions.
Blending rather than grinding, which gives a smooth paste instead of texture.
Refined oil in place of red palm oil.
Skipping the eggs, which are structural rather than decorative.
sources: Adapted from 'One Dish Ghanaians have abandoned and Missing Out Its Health Benefits', byline as printed 'By Pamela Ofori-Boateng', modernghana.com, 17 September 2017.

Ingredients exactly as printed: 3 slightly ripe plantains; 3 chili peppers; Salt to taste; 1 medium onion; 7 tablespoons palm oil; Roasted groundnuts; 2 eggs; 1 avocado; Dried smoked herrings and 'koobi' (optional). NOTE that the groundnuts and the herring/koobi carry no quantities at all.

Method as printed: boil plantains and eggs 30 minutes with salt; grind the onions, peppers and groundnuts; add herring and koobi and grind in an earthenware bowl; mash the plantains separately; heat sliced onions in 5-6 tablespoons palm oil; mix the palm oil into the plantain; combine; garnish.

QUANTITY INCONSISTENCY, flagged and NOT silently corrected: the ingredient list gives 7 tablespoons of palm oil while the method uses 5-6 tablespoons for the onions and then adds further oil to the plantain. The two do not reconcile. The tip above treats 7 as the total and starts at 5, which is an editorial reading of the discrepancy, stated as such.
The page's own steps say 'pear' for the garnish, which in Ghanaian English means avocado; rendered as avocado above.
CULTURAL NOTE, from the same page: traditionally served to brides the morning before weddings with eggs, and described as 'the local version of a birthday cake' for birthday celebrants.

ON THE CEREMONIAL FORM, from Fran Osseo-Asare, Gastronomica, Winter 2002, byline 'By Fran Osseo-Asare', verbatim: 'Oto, a sacred dish made from hard-boiled eggs, mashed yam, and palm oil, is an Akan as well as a Ga tradition.' And: 'Oto is given without salt or pepper' for ceremonial uses. NOTE she describes the YAM form; this recipe is the PLANTAIN form.

COMMUNITY DISAGREEMENT, unreconciled: Osseo-Asare calls oto 'an Akan as well as a Ga tradition'. ghanaremembers.com (no byline, no date, no recipe) says Otor is prepared by the GaDangme for special occasions and is sometimes offered 'without salt and pepper, as a form of thanks' to spirits — a Ga-only attribution. Neither is treated as settling the question.

BASE-STARCH DISAGREEMENT, also unreconciled: this source and a 2019 Ghana Broadcasting Corporation piece ('Etor – Mashed plantain') use PLANTAIN; the yam versions are at GHA008 and GHA009. Both starches are published under their own entries rather than merged.

A NAME CONFLICT WORTH RECORDING: the Africa News Cookbook compilation uses 'Eto' for PLANTAIN FRITTERS — 2-3 overripe medium plantains, 1 small onion, 25-50g self-raising flour, 5ml palm oil optional, salt and hot pepper, stood 20 minutes and fried until golden brown — which is a completely different preparation from the mash this entry describes. That fritter is not published here as eto, because three other sources use the name for the mash.
storage: 2 days refrigerated. The palm oil will solidify and the colour deepens.
reheating: Gentle heat, or let it come to room temperature. Do not microwave hard.
healthBenefits: Red palm oil is one of the richest known food sources of provitamin-A carotenoids and vitamin E tocotrienols.
Groundnuts and eggs together make this a complete-protein dish.
Plantain supplies potassium and resistant starch.
Avocado adds monounsaturated fat and folate.
culturalNote: Eto is what you are given at the thresholds of a life — the morning of a wedding, a birthday, the naming of a child — and the eggs on top are the marker that this is an occasion rather than a meal. Its author's framing is that Ghanaians have abandoned it, which is itself worth recording: this is a dish being written about because it is slipping away.
